title: Prove It: Long Division Detective
goal: I can solve long division word problems, find the mistake in someone's work, and check my answer by multiplying.

card.desc: Prove-it day for long division. Bailey solves mixed 2- and 3-digit problems, decides when a story needs dividing or multiplying, finds and fixes the mistake in someone else's worked problem, and convinces Jonathan with a multiply-back check. Seven new words, including algorithm and discrepancy.

win: Long division detective: you solved it, checked it, and caught every mistake!

slides.title: Prove It: Long Division Detective
slides.text: This week you learned the long division algorithm with 2-digit and 3-digit numbers. Today you prove it: solve word problems, find mistakes in someone else's work, and check every answer by multiplying.

notes.do: Set out: whiteboard and marker with the four steps written on it, paper and pencil, 3 index cards with the word problems from slide 11 written on them, her book. Base-ten blocks nearby in case she needs them.
notes.say: "Prove-it day. You are the teacher today: you will check other people's work and find their mistakes."
notes.ask: "How did Tuesday's Show What You Know go? Did the Lesson 13 packet feel easy or hard?" (Check her scores and the packet before class.)

slides.title: Hiccup's test
slides.text: Think about How to Train Your Dragon.
prompts: What test do the young Vikings have to pass to become full members of the tribe? How is Hiccup doing so far?
What is one mistake Hiccup made? How did he try to fix it?
Do you think Hiccup will pass? Use a clue from the book to back up your prediction.
starters: Hiccup made a mistake when … He tried to fix it by …

notes.do: 6 minutes. Let her find the pages.
notes.ask: "What mistake did Hiccup make, and how did he try to fix it?" This links to today: finding and fixing mistakes.
notes.listen: A prediction backed by a clue from the text, not just a wish. If she only says "yes he will", ask: "What in the book makes you think so?"

slides.title: Words for today
slides.text: Tap each card to flip it. Read it out loud. Then use it in your own sentence.

words.meaning: A set of steps that always works when you follow them in order.
words.example: Long division is an algorithm: divide, multiply, subtract, bring down.

words.meaning: A difference between two things that should match.
words.example: 13 × 6 = 78, not 618. That discrepancy tells me there is a mistake.

words.meaning: Careful and complete, checking every part.
words.example: A thorough check looks at every step, not just the answer.

words.meaning: To fix a mistake and make it right.
words.example: Fishlegs found his subtraction slip and rectified it.

words.meaning: To make someone believe that something is true.
words.example: Show the multiplication check to convince me your answer is right.

words.meaning: A test or ceremony a person goes through to become a full member of a group.
words.example: In the book, the young Vikings must train a dragon as part of their initiation into the tribe.

words.meaning: To decide something after thinking about the facts.
words.example: 168 × 4 = 672, so I conclude that my answer is right.

notes.do: She reads each card and makes her own sentence. Write discrepancy and rectify on the whiteboard.
notes.say: "Today's words are detective words. You will find a discrepancy, rectify it, and convince me you are right."
notes.ask: "Why is long division called an algorithm?" (It is a set of steps that always works.) "What is Hiccup's initiation?"
notes.listen: Discrepancy: two things that should match but don't. Thorough: every part checked.

slides.title: Is it a division story?
slides.text: A story is division when a total is split into equal groups. Then follow these steps.

steps.text: Read: Stoick shares 456 fish equally among 8 dragons. How many fish does each dragon get?
Decide: a total (456) is split into equal groups (8 dragons). Divide: 456 ÷ 8.
Estimate: 8 × 50 = 400 and 8 × 60 = 480. The answer is between 50 and 60.
Solve: 8 does not fit in 4, so start with 45.
Check and label: 57 × 8 = 400 + 56 = 456. Each dragon gets 57 fish.

slides.tip: If the story puts equal groups together to find a total, that is multiplication, not division.

notes.do: She solves 456 ÷ 8 on paper before you reveal Step 4.
notes.say: Praise each step she does: "Estimate, yes." "45 first, yes."
notes.ask: "What does the 57 count?" (fish for each dragon.)
notes.listen: She labels the answer. A bare 57 is not an answer to a story.

items.q: Stoick has 5 ships. Each ship carries 128 Vikings. How many Vikings are there in all? Which number sentence solves it?
items.why: Equal groups put together: multiply. 128 × 5 = 640 Vikings.
no: The groups are equal, so adding the two numbers does not work.
Nothing is taken away in this story, so do not subtract.
This story puts groups together to find a total, so multiply.

items.q: The Hooligans pack 738 arrows equally into 6 barrels. How many arrows go in each barrel?
items.no: Write the division, then solve it on paper one step at a time.

items.q: Hiccup is reading a book with 144 pages. He reads 8 pages a night. How many nights will it take?
items.no: Write the division, then solve it on paper one step at a time.

notes.do: She says divide or multiply and why BEFORE she solves. Then she solves on paper.
notes.ask: "Is a total being split, or are groups being put together?"
notes.listen: Ships item: "Groups are put together, so multiply." 738 ÷ 6 = 123 arrows. 144 ÷ 8 = 18 nights (8 does not fit in 1, so start with 14).

slides.title: Find the mistake
slides.text: Fishlegs worked out 672 ÷ 4 and got 165 R 2. Be a thorough detective.

steps.text: Check by multiplying: 165 × 4 + 2 = 660 + 2 = 662. But the dividend is 672. That is a discrepancy, so there is a mistake.
Go step by step. 6 − 4 = 2 ✔. Bring down 7: 27 ✔. 6 × 4 = 24 ✔. 27 − 24 = 2 ✘. It should be 3.
Check again: 168 × 4 = 400 + 240 + 32 = 672 ✔. Now I can conclude it is right.

slides.tip: The check tells you THAT there is a mistake. Going step by step tells you WHERE.

notes.do: Before Step 2, let her hunt for the mistake on her own. Give her one full minute.
notes.say: When she finds it: "You found it! That is exactly what a thorough mathematician does."
notes.ask: "Was the multiplication check enough to find the mistake?" (No, it shows there IS one. Then you look step by step.)
notes.listen: She checks every subtraction out loud, not just the last one.

items.q: Snotlout worked out 936 ÷ 9 and got 14. Check: 14 × 9 = 126, not 936. Find the mistake in the work.
choices: Nothing is wrong. The answer is accurate.
A placeholder 0 is missing in the quotient. The answer is 104.
items.why: A placeholder 0 is missing in the quotient. The answer is 104. Fix it and finish: 936 ÷ 9 = 104. Check: 104 × 9 = 936.
no: 2 × 9 = 18. That is too big.
Check: 14 × 9 = 126, not 936. That discrepancy means there is a mistake.
Check it: that subtraction is correct.

items.q: Hiccup worked out 952 ÷ 7 and got 131 R 5. Check: 131 × 7 + 5 = 922, not 952. Find the mistake in the work.
choices: A placeholder 0 is missing in the quotient.
He forgot to bring down a digit.
Nothing is wrong. The answer is accurate.
items.why: The multiplication is wrong: 3 × 7 = 21, not 24. Fix it and finish: 952 ÷ 7 = 136. Check: 136 × 7 = 952.
no: Every place in the quotient has a digit. Check each multiplication.
Every digit was brought down. Check each multiplication.
Check: 131 × 7 + 5 = 922, not 952. That discrepancy means there is a mistake.

notes.do: She reads the work out loud line by line and says ✔ or ✘ for each step.
notes.say: Praise every correct ✔ she gives, and cheer loudly when she finds the ✘.
notes.listen: 936 ÷ 9: Snotlout skipped the 0 when 9 did not fit in 3 (answer 104). 952 ÷ 7: 3 × 7 is 21, not 24 (answer 136).

slides.title: Convince me: check with the area model
slides.text: To check a 3-digit quotient, multiply it back. The area model makes it quick. Check 942 ÷ 6 = 157:
slides.tip: 600 + 300 + 42 = 942. It matches the dividend, so the answer is accurate.

notes.do: She draws the three boxes on the whiteboard herself.
notes.listen: She adds the three parts correctly: 600 + 300 = 900, plus 42 = 942.

items.q: Convince me: check 738 ÷ 6 = 123 by multiplying. 123 × 6 = ____
items.no: Break 123 apart: 100 + 20 + 3. Multiply each part by 6, then add.

items.q: Convince me: check 832 ÷ 8 = 104 by multiplying. 104 × 8 = ____
items.no: Break 104 apart: 100 + 4. Multiply each part by 8, then add.

notes.say: Praise each box she multiplies correctly.

items.no: Write the division, then solve it on paper one step at a time.

items.q: 612 eggs are shared equally among 6 dragon nests. How many eggs are in each nest?
items.no: Write the division, then solve it on paper one step at a time.

items.no: Write the division, then solve it on paper one step at a time.

notes.do: The three stories are on index cards, face down. She picks one at a time and does the whole routine at the whiteboard.
notes.say: Praise each part of the routine as she does it: "Decided, yes. Estimated, yes. Checked, yes!"
notes.listen: 630 ÷ 3 = 210 piles (the last 0 must be written). 612 ÷ 6 = 102 eggs (placeholder 0). 336 ÷ 7 = 48 days (7 does not fit in 3).

slides.title: How to find a mistake
slides.text: Tap the steps in the order a thorough detective uses them.
steps: Notice the discrepancy: it does not match the dividend.
Go back to the first step of the work.
Check each divide, multiply, subtract and bring down.
Rectify the wrong step and finish the problem.
slides.why: Check, notice, go back, look step by step, rectify, check again.
slides.hint: You cannot know there is a mistake until you check. What comes first?

notes.do: She says the steps from memory before tapping.
notes.listen: Check first, rectify near the end, check again last.

items.q: Fishlegs's answer was 165 R 2, but the check gave 662 instead of 672. What is the difference between 662 and 672 called?
items.why: A discrepancy is a difference between two things that should match.
no: An algorithm is a set of steps.
An initiation is a test to join a group.
The quotient is the answer to a division.

items.q: Fishlegs found his mistake and fixed it. He ____ it. (Use a word from your word cards that means fixed. Add -ed.)
items.why: To rectify is to fix a mistake. He rectified it.
items.no: It starts with rect- and ends with -ified.

items.q: Which is a thorough check?
choices: Looking only at the final answer
Checking every step and then multiplying back
items.why: Thorough means careful and complete, checking every part.
no: That skips the steps.
Guessing is not checking.
Asking someone else is not checking it yourself.

notes.ask: "Use convince in a sentence about your math." "Use conclude in a sentence about the book."
notes.listen: She uses each word correctly in her own sentence.

slides.title: Your weekend plan
slides.text: You proved it: you can do the long division algorithm, use it in word problems, and find other people's mistakes.

Friday: the Lesson 15 Practice and page 2 of the Lesson 14 Packet.

teacher.objective: Bailey proves the week: mixed long division with no remainder (2- and 3-digit dividends, placeholder zeros, first digit too small), deciding when a story is division (a total split into equal groups) or multiplication, finding and rectifying the mistake in a worked problem (subtraction slip, wrong fact, omitted zero), and checking every quotient by multiplying back with the area model.
materials: Class lesson on your laptop or tablet (teacher code 9110)
Whiteboard and marker with the four steps written on it
3 index cards, each with one word problem from class slide 11 (630 shields in piles of 3; 612 eggs in 6 nests; 336 fish, 7 a day)
Paper and a pencil for Bailey
Base-ten blocks nearby, only if she needs them
Her book, How to Train Your Dragon

plan.do: Class slide 1. Index cards face down, whiteboard ready. Ask about Tuesday's check and the Lesson 13 packet.
Class slide 2. The young Vikings' test, one mistake Hiccup made and how he fixed it, a prediction with a clue.
Class slide 3. 95 ÷ 5 and 832 ÷ 8 on paper; praise the placeholder 0.
Class slide 4. Her own sentence for each word; discrepancy and rectify on the whiteboard.
Class slides 5–6. 456 fish among 8 dragons (decide, estimate, solve, check, label); then divide or multiply, 738 ÷ 6 and 144 ÷ 8.
Class slides 7–8. Fishlegs's 672 ÷ 4 = 165 R 2: check, discrepancy, step by step, rectify. Then Snotlout's missing zero and Hiccup's wrong fact. Praise each ✔ she gives.
Class slides 9–10. Check 942 ÷ 6 = 157 with three area boxes; then she checks 123 × 6 and 104 × 8.
Class slide 11. She picks each index card and does the whole routine at the whiteboard.
Class slide 12. She orders the six detective steps from memory.
Class slide 13. Discrepancy, rectified, thorough; convince and conclude in her own sentences.
Class slide 14. 864 ÷ 6, the apples story, Snotlout's 728 ÷ 7 on her own; note any miss.
Class slide 15. Course page: Lesson 15 task list and the three Long Division Lane links.

watch: Dividing in a story that needs multiplying (5 ships with 128 Vikings each). Ask: "Is a total being split, or are groups being put together?"
A bare number for a story answer. Ask: "57 what?" until she labels it.
Checking only the final answer when hunting for a mistake. Say: "The check tells you THAT. Now find WHERE: read me every subtraction."
Omitting the 0 at the end of a quotient (630 ÷ 3 = 21). Ask: "Did you bring down every digit? What happened to the last 0?"
In the area-model check, multiplying 1 × 6 instead of 100 × 6 for the hundreds box. Point to the place value.
"I can't do it" on a story. Say: "Read it to me. Is a total being split?" Then praise that first decision before the next step.

packet_key.answer: algorithm → steps that always work in order; discrepancy → a difference that should not be there; thorough → careful and complete; rectify → to fix a mistake; convince → to make someone believe something; initiation → a test to join a group; conclude → to decide after thinking about the facts

teacher.notes: Bailey takes Show What You Know on her own tonight at the end of the After-class lesson. Check her Formspree score before Monday. If she scores under 90, look at the misses: computation (placeholder zero, first digit too small), stories (divide or multiply), or mistake-finding. Open Monday with 8 minutes on that one part, then she retakes (a brand-new question set). Monday starts remainders, which needs a solid algorithm, so reteach computation first if more than one area slipped.
